problem: Social navigation research spans robotics, HRI, multi-agent systems, graphics and psychology, with no shared vocabulary; papers are hard to compare, and conflict handling between robots and pedestrians is not separated from general collision avoidance.
motivation: Mobile robots are still rare in homes and offices partly because navigating around people is hard and each community defines it differently. A common language for conflicts (situations where a collision occurs unless someone changes direction or speed) would let researchers place, compare and benchmark work.
key_idea: Define conflict avoidance as the survey scope, introduce a 7-attribute taxonomy (robot role, number of agents, observability, motion control, communication, experiment type, agent type), and map 112 papers onto it.
insight: Papers differ widely on the taxonomy attributes, and these attributes determine which evaluation metrics apply (e.g. group formation needs more than one pedestrian). Results on communication cues conflict across studies (gaze cues effective in Hart et al. and Khambhaita et al., not in Fiore et al. and May et al.), which the survey attributes to differences in how the signal was implemented. Roughly 39 of 75 surveyed papers used only or partly simulation, so many conclusions may not transfer to real-world embodied social navigation. This is a survey; there are no ablations.
method: Scope definition: three requirements (autonomous agent with a reachable goal, humans/animals present, real-world interaction) plus a formal conflict definition, and a distinction between conflict and collision.

Paper collection: snowballing from existing surveys [17, 78] via Google Scholar citations, keeping one paper per research group unless the taxonomy classifies them differently; 112 papers selected, and 54 of the 166 citations do not meet all three requirements.

Taxonomy: seven attributes with values (Role R/I/B/N; Abs/Density; Full/Partial/Depth/RGB; SFM/ORCA/ROS/Human/Other; communication None/Indirect/Direct; Sim/Lab/ItW/Survey; H-R/H-A/H-H/R-R/Hom/Het), arranged in a dependency hierarchy.
Models (Sec. 3): multiagent systems (ORCA, POMDPs, crowd simulation), human-inspired/psychology models (GMA, IPS, personal space, IRL), and physics-based models (SFM extensions, potential fields).

Algorithms (Sec. 4): inferring human trajectories (online and offline/IRL/DRL such as CADRL, SARL), conveying robot intent (LEDs, projections, gaze, legibility), and mediating conflicts (motion effort, person following).

Evaluation (Sec. 5): metrics grouped as interaction properties, actions, emergent behaviors, algorithmic properties and subjective surveys, each linked to relevant taxonomy attributes, plus simulators and benchmarks.

Checklist and open problems: a six-point checklist (taxonomy, reliability, human presence, context, success, evaluation) and open problems (metric standardization, context awareness, groups, adaptive/lifelong learning).
numbers_note: Survey paper with no experimental results; the tables give taxonomy attribute values, not performance numbers.
results: The survey maps 112 conflict-avoidance papers onto a 7-attribute taxonomy across models (multiagent, human-inspired, physics-based) and algorithms (inference, intent-conveying, mediation). It also catalogues evaluation metrics and produces a design checklist. It has no quantitative results or baselines.
limitations: Excludes simulation-only, multi-robot-only and non-conflict social tasks (following, queuing), and covers only a curated subset of the literature.
Some relevant concepts (collision type, context awareness, group navigation, social cues vs. signals, human vs. robot reactions) are left out of the taxonomy as not yet mature.
Little coverage of vision-language or learned end-to-end embodied navigation; the survey is mostly pre-2022 and is not an embodied navigation benchmark study.
builds_on: Kruse et al. 2013 social navigation survey
Rios-Martinez et al. 2015 socially-aware navigation survey
